title: Analytical Thinking
description: Break messy problems into pieces, estimate fast, spot patterns, read data honestly and make decisions you can explain.
keyIdeas: Split a big problem into a **MECE** tree (no overlaps, no gaps) and dig into the branch that moved the most.
Estimate by chaining friendly factors; landing within a factor of 2–3 is often enough to decide.
Ask what changes and what stays the same: add the same → linear, multiply by the same → exponential.
Before trusting a number, check the axis, the average (mean or median?) and the denominator.
Fix root causes, not symptoms: keep asking *why* until the fix stops the problem coming back.
Decide with explicit criteria and weights; move fast through two-way doors, slow down at one-way doors.

concepts.label: Issue tree
concepts.summary: Split a big question into smaller sub-questions (e.g. profit = revenue − costs) and dig into the branch that moved the most.

concepts.label: MECE
concepts.summary: A split is MECE when its branches are mutually exclusive (no overlaps) and collectively exhaustive (no gaps).

concepts.label: Fermi estimate
concepts.summary: Estimate an unknown by breaking it into factors you can guess, rounding and multiplying; within a factor of 2–3 is often enough to decide.

concepts.label: Friendly numbers
concepts.summary: Round each factor to one significant figure, multiply the front digits and count the zeros.

concepts.label: Sanity check
concepts.summary: Ask whether a number is plausible, roughly the right size, before trusting it; being off by 10× is a red flag.

concepts.label: Work backwards
concepts.summary: When you know how something ended, start at the end and undo each step, last one first, then check forwards.

concepts.label: Balance method
concepts.summary: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other, until x stands alone.

concepts.label: Solve a smaller version
concepts.summary: When a problem is big, solve tiny versions first and look for the pattern that scales up.

concepts.label: Spot the pattern
concepts.summary: Ask what changes and what stays the same: a constant difference means linear, a constant ratio means exponential.
aliases: what changes what stays the same

concepts.label: Linear growth
concepts.summary: Adding the same amount each step.

concepts.label: Exponential growth
concepts.summary: Multiplying by the same factor each step; it starts slow but always overtakes linear growth in the end.

concepts.label: Mean vs median
concepts.summary: The mean is dragged by extreme values; the median (the middle value) shows what is typical.

concepts.label: Misleading axis
concepts.summary: A bar chart whose axis starts above zero makes small differences look huge.

concepts.label: Rates, not counts
concepts.summary: Compare groups of different sizes by rate (per person, per 1,000), always asking "out of how many?"

concepts.label: Root cause
concepts.summary: Why a problem keeps happening, as opposed to the symptom you notice; fixing it stops the problem coming back.

concepts.label: 5 whys
concepts.summary: Keep asking "why?" from the problem down through causes, past blame, until you reach a fix that stops it recurring.

concepts.label: Weighted scorecard
concepts.summary: Score each option on weighted criteria, multiply and add, then compare the totals with your gut.

concepts.label: One-way vs two-way doors
concepts.summary: Decide fast on easy-to-reverse choices (two-way doors) and slow down on hard-to-undo ones (one-way doors).

concepts.label: Second-order effects
concepts.summary: The knock-on consequences of the direct result; keep asking "and then what?"

concepts.label: Goodhart's law
concepts.summary: When a measure becomes a target, people game it and it stops measuring what you cared about.

concepts.label: Elimination
concepts.summary: List every possibility, let each clue cross some out, and when stuck assume one and look for a contradiction.

concepts.label: Contrapositive
concepts.summary: An if-then clue "if P then Q" also means "if not Q then not P", and is broken only when P holds and Q does not.

units.title: Break it down
units.description: Turn one fuzzy question into small ones you can answer, and put a rough number on anything.

lessons.title: Slice the problem: issue trees
lessons.takeaway: Split a fuzzy problem into a tree of smaller questions with no overlaps and no gaps (MECE), then dig into the branch that moved the most.

steps.title: Meet Juno's café
steps.body:
Juno runs a small café, and this month she's worried: **profit is down**. *Why?* is too big to answer in one go.

So slice it. Profit = revenue − costs, so the first question becomes: *is revenue down, or are costs up?* Revenue = customers × average spend, so that branch splits again.

That branching map is an **issue tree**: the big question at the top, small questions you can check with data at the bottom.

steps.prompt: Put Juno's questions in order, from the big question at the top of the tree down to the most specific one she could check tomorrow.
items: Why is profit down this month?
Is revenue down, or are costs up?
Revenue: fewer customers, or less spent per customer?
Customers: fewer new faces, or fewer regulars coming back?
Regulars: on which days did they stop coming?
steps.hint: Ask of each question: which bigger question is this one part of?
steps.explanation: Each question is one branch of the question above it. **Profit** splits into revenue and costs; **revenue** into customers × spend; **customers** into new faces and regulars; and **regulars** into something concrete enough to look up in the till records. The bottom of a good tree is always a question you can answer with data.

steps.title: MECE: no overlaps, no gaps
steps.body:
A good split is **MECE** (say *mee-see*), a term from management consulting:

- **Mutually exclusive**: the branches don't overlap, so nothing is counted twice.
- **Collectively exhaustive**: together they cover everything, so no cause can hide in a gap.

*Weekdays / weekends* is MECE: every visit lands in exactly one. *Under 30 / over 20* overlaps: a 25-year-old is in both. *Coffee / cakes* has a gap: where do tea and sandwiches go?

A catch-all branch like **everything else** is a cheap way to close gaps.

steps.prompt: Theo, Juno's barista, drafts some splits for her tree. The café is open 7:00–18:00, seven days a week. Sort each split.
buckets: Overlaps: something lands in two branches
Gaps: something lands in no branch

items.text: Visits: weekdays / weekends
Customers: first visit ever / been before
Revenue: drinks / food / everything else
Customers: under 18 / 18 and over
Ages: under 30 / over 20
Drinks: coffee drinks / drinks with milk / drinks without milk
Revenue: coffee / cakes
Customers: under 18 / over 65
Days: Monday–Thursday / Saturday–Sunday

steps.hint: For each split, look for one thing that fits two branches, then for one thing that fits none.
steps.explanation: **MECE** splits put every visit, customer or dollar in exactly one branch; *everything else* is what makes the revenue split complete. **Overlaps:** 25-year-olds sit in both age groups, 11:00–12:00 is in both time slots, and a latte is both a coffee drink and a drink with milk. **Gaps:** tea and sandwiches have no branch, nobody aged 18–65 does, and Friday is missing entirely. Overlaps make you double-count; gaps let the real cause hide.

steps.title: Find the branch that moved
steps.problem: Juno's revenue fell from **$9,600** to **$8,050**. Last month: 1,200 customers spending $8.00 on average. This month: 1,150 customers spending $7.00. Which branch explains most of the drop?
steps: Use the tree: revenue = customers × average spend. 1,200 × $8 = $9,600 and 1,150 × $7 = $8,050, a drop of **$1,550**.
Change one branch at a time. If only customers had changed: 1,150 × $8 = $9,200, a drop of just **$400**.
The rest comes from spend: 1,150 × ($8 − $7) = **$1,150**.
steps.answer: About three-quarters of the drop sits in the **average spend** branch, so that's where Juno digs next, not in a hunt for new customers.

steps.prompt: Juno's lunch counter: last month **800 customers** spent **$10.00** each on average. This month **600 customers** spent **$10.50**. What's this month's lunch revenue?
steps.explanation: Revenue = customers × average spend = 600 × $10.50 = **$6,300**, down $1,700 from 800 × $10 = $8,000.

steps.prompt: Same lunch counter: revenue fell from $8,000 to $6,300. Which branch should Juno dig into first?
choices: Customers: losing 200 people explains the whole drop
Average spend, because it changed this month
Both equally: always investigate every branch at the same depth
Neither: start a fresh tree with different branches
steps.hint: Work out what each branch alone did to revenue, like in the example.
steps.explanation: Change one branch at a time. Losing 200 customers at $10 each costs **$2,000**. The higher spend *adds* 600 × $0.50 = **$300**. So 8,000 − 2,000 + 300 = 6,300: the whole drop, and then some, is in the customers branch. Spend changed too, but in the helpful direction.

lessons.title: Fermi estimates: good-enough numbers, fast
lessons.takeaway: Break an unknown number into factors you can guess, round to friendly numbers, multiply, and sanity-check the order of magnitude.

steps.title: Guess like a physicist
steps.body:
How many cafés can a city of 500,000 people support? Nobody hands you that number, but you can **estimate** it in a minute.

Physicist Enrico Fermi was famous for questions like this. The recipe:

- **Break** the unknown into factors you can guess.
- **Round** each to a friendly number.
- **Multiply**, then **sanity-check** against something you know.

You're after the right **order of magnitude**: tens, hundreds or thousands? Landing within a factor of 2 or 3 is a good result.

steps.prompt: Juno wonders if her city of 500,000 has room for another café. Put Theo's estimate in order, from the starting fact to the answer.
items: Start with what you know: 500,000 people
About half drink coffee on a given day → 250,000 coffee drinkers
About 2 cups each → 500,000 cups a day
About 1 cup in 5 is bought at a café → 100,000 café coffees a day
A busy café sells about 250 a day → room for about 400 cafés
steps.hint: Each step uses the number produced by the step before it.
steps.explanation: Each step takes the number from the step before and multiplies by one guessed factor: 500,000 × ½ × 2 × ⅕ ÷ 250 = **400**. Every factor is a rough assumption, and that's fine: you can see exactly which guess to question. The useful part is the scale: *hundreds* of cafés. If the city already has 1,000, the market is probably crowded.

steps.title: Friendly numbers
steps.body:
Round each factor to **one significant figure** (like 2, 5 or 300), multiply the front digits, then count the zeros.

- 312 × 48 → 300 × 50 = **15,000** (exact: 14,976)
- 1,900 × 21 → 2,000 × 20 = **40,000** (exact: 39,900)

When you can, round one factor up and the other down, so the errors partly cancel.

steps.prompt: Estimate **3,800 × 52** with friendly numbers. Anything from 150,000 to 250,000 counts.
steps.explanation: 3,800 → 4,000 and 52 → 50, so 4 × 5 = 20 with four zeros: **200,000**. The exact answer is 197,600, about 1% away. This question accepts 150,000–250,000 because the skill is speed, not the last digit.

steps.title: Beans for a month
steps.problem: Juno's café sells about **250 coffees a day**. Roughly how many kilograms of beans does she need per month?
steps: Cups per month: 250 × 30 = **7,500**.
Beans per cup: a double shot uses roughly 15–20 g. Take the friendly **20 g**.
Sanity check: at 20 g a cup, a 1 kg bag makes 50 coffees, so 250 coffees use 5 bags a day. For a busy café, that sounds right.
steps.answer: About **150 kg** a month: the order should be in the low hundreds of kilos, not tens or thousands.

steps.prompt: Your turn, with your own assumptions. Roughly how many times does a human heart beat in an **80-year** life? Type the whole number, like 2000000000 or 2e9. Anything from 1.5 billion to 4.5 billion counts.
steps.hint: Beats per minute → per day (1,440 minutes) → per year (365 days) → × 80. A resting heart beats roughly 60–100 times a minute.
steps.explanation: Friendly chain: about 70 beats a minute × 1,440 minutes a day ≈ **100,000 beats a day**. × 365 ≈ 37 million a year. × 80 ≈ **3 billion**. Assume 60 beats a minute and you get about 2.5 billion; assume 100 and you get about 4.2 billion. All are fine Fermi answers. The win is knowing it's *billions*, not millions or trillions.

steps.prompt: Sanity check! Sort each claim: plausible, or off by about 10× or more?

items.text: A city of 500,000 people has a few hundred cafés
A typical adult walks 5,000–10,000 steps a day
A car is driven about 15,000 km a year
A person blinks about 15,000 times a day
A person drinks about 200 litres of water a day
One small café sells 50,000 coffees a day
A smartphone weighs about 2 kg
There are about 500 seconds in a day
A heart beats about 3,000 times in a lifetime
A school bus seats about 5 people

steps.hint: Compare each claim with something you know well: your own day, your own body, your own phone.
steps.explanation: Quick anchors catch these. **Too high:** people drink about 2 litres a day, not 200; 50,000 coffees in a 12-hour day is about 70 a minute; a phone weighs about 0.2 kg. **Too low:** a day has 24 × 3,600 = 86,400 seconds; a heart beats about 100,000 times in a *single day*; school buses seat dozens. **Plausible:** blinking 15–20 times a minute for 16 waking hours is roughly 15,000–19,000 blinks, and the steps, kilometres and cafés are in the right range.

steps.prompt: Your Fermi estimate rests on five guessed factors. You have 10 minutes to improve it. Which factor should you research first?
choices: The one you're least sure about, since it could be off by the biggest factor
The first one in the chain, since everything builds on it
The one with the biggest number
None: researching defeats the point of a Fermi estimate
steps.explanation: The final answer is a product, so a factor that's off by 5× makes the answer off by 5×. Check the guess with the **widest uncertainty** first; refining a factor you already know well barely moves the result. Position in the chain and size of the number don't matter.

lessons.title: Work backwards, simplify first
lessons.takeaway: When you know the end, start there and undo each step in reverse; when a problem is big, solve a tiny version first and look for the pattern.

steps.title: Start at the finish
steps.body:
Some puzzles tell you how things **ended** and ask how they started. Don't guess forwards: start at the end and **undo** each step, last one first.

- added → subtract
- subtracted → add
- doubled → halve

Then run the story forwards to check.

steps.title: The till mystery
steps.problem: Juno put some cash in the till at opening. The morning rush **doubled** it, she **paid $30** to the milk supplier, then **took in $14** more. At closing there's **$84**. How much did she start with?
steps: Start at the end: **$84**.
Undo the last step (+$14): 84 − 14 = **$70**.
Undo the doubling: 100 ÷ 2 = **$50**.
Check forwards: 50 × 2 − 30 + 14 = 84 ✓

steps.prompt: Theo's loyalty points: he started with some, a promo **tripled** them, he **spent 40** on a free cake, then **earned 20**. Now he has **100**. Put the undo moves in order.
items: Check by running the story forwards
steps.hint: The last thing that happened is the first thing to undo.
steps.explanation: Undo in **reverse** order: the last thing that happened (earning 20) is the first thing to undo. Each move is the opposite operation: earned → subtract, spent → add, tripled → divide by 3. Finish by running the story forwards to catch slips.

steps.prompt: So how many points did Theo start with?

steps.title: Keep it balanced
steps.body:
Juno's kitchen scale balances with **3 bags of flour and 4 kg of weights** on the left, and **1 bag and 12 kg** on the right. How heavy is one bag?

Treat it like a real balance: **whatever you do to one side, do to the other**, and it stays level. Take a bag off both sides, then take weights off both sides, until one bag sits alone.

steps.prompt: Each bag weighs x kg, so 3x + 4 = x + 12. Get x alone by making the same move on both sides.
steps.hint: First get the bags on one side only, then the weights on the other.
steps.explanation: Take one bag off each side: 2x + 4 = 12. Take 4 kg off each side: 2x = 8. Halve both sides: **x = 4 kg**. Check: 3 × 4 + 4 = 16 and 4 + 12 = 16 ✓

steps.prompt: Theo's riddle: *Five times my number, minus 6, equals twice my number plus 9.* That's 5x − 6 = 2x + 9. Find his number.
steps.hint: A minus 6 is undone by adding 6 to both sides.
steps.explanation: Subtract 2x from both sides: 3x − 6 = 9. Add 6 to both sides: 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3: **x = 5**. Check: 5 × 5 − 6 = 19 and 2 × 5 + 9 = 19 ✓

steps.title: Shrink the problem
steps.body:
Stuck on something big? Solve a **tiny version** first and look for the pattern.

At Juno's staff party, everyone clinks glasses once with everyone else. How many clinks for 10 people? Try small:

- 2 people → 1 clink
- 3 people → 3 clinks
- 4 people → 6 clinks

Each newcomer clinks with everyone already there: +1, then +2, then +3…

steps.prompt: How many clinks for **10 people**?
steps.hint: The 5th person adds 4 clinks, the 6th adds 5… keep going to the 10th.
steps.explanation: Keep adding: 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 9 = **45**. The pattern also gives a shortcut: each of 10 people clinks with 9 others, but that counts every clink twice, so 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45. Small cases first, then the pattern, then the formula.

units.title: Read the signal
units.description: Spot patterns, read charts and averages without being fooled, and trace problems to their roots.

lessons.title: What changes, what stays the same
lessons.takeaway: Ask what changes and what stays the same: a constant difference means linear (add), a constant ratio means exponential (multiply), and exponential wins in the end.

steps.title: Two questions
steps.body:
Faced with a list of numbers, ask: **what changes, and what stays the same?**

- Subtract neighbours. If the **difference** stays the same, it's **linear**: you add the same amount each step. 4, 7, 10, 13 → +3 every time.
- If the differences grow, divide neighbours. If the **ratio** stays the same, it's **exponential** (also called geometric): you multiply by the same amount. 3, 6, 12, 24 → ×2 every time.

steps.prompt: Weekly sign-ups to Juno's newsletter: **12, 19, 26, 33**, … If the pattern holds, how many sign up in week 5?
steps.explanation: The differences are all 7, so it's linear: 33 + 7 = **40**.

steps.prompt: Sort each sequence by what stays the same.
steps.hint: Subtract neighbours first. If that's not constant, divide them.
steps.explanation: **Linear:** +3, −10 and +0.25 each step; adding a negative still counts. **Exponential:** ×2, ×½ and ×10; halving is multiplying too. **Neither:** 1, 4, 9, 16 are the squares (differences 3, 5, 7 grow by 2, but no ratio is constant); 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 adds the two previous numbers; 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 are the primes. Patterns can follow other rules, so test the difference first, then the ratio, and only then hunt for something else.

steps.prompt: Juno's latte-art video spreads: **3, 6, 12, 24** people share it in hours 1, 2, 3 and 4. If the pattern holds, how many share it in **hour 7**?
steps.hint: Keep doubling for hours 5, 6 and 7.
steps.explanation: The ratio is always 2, so keep doubling: 48, 96, **192**. In one step: 3 × 2⁶ = 192.

steps.prompt: Juno's savings at the end of each year: **$500, $600, $720, $864**. What changes and what stays the same? Predict year 5.
steps.hint: The differences grow (100, 120, 144). Try dividing neighbours instead.
steps.explanation: The differences grow (100, 120, 144), so it isn't linear. The ratios are all **1.2**: savings grow 20% a year. 864 × 1.2 = **$1,036.80**. Assuming it's linear and adding the last gap again would give $1,008, an underestimate that grows every year.

steps.title: Linear vs exponential
steps.body:
Theo is offered two summer deals for 30 days:

- **A**: $100 every day.
- **B**: 1 cent on day 1, then double the day before.

A looks safe. B starts embarrassingly small: on day 7 it pays 64 cents. But linear growth **adds**, while exponential growth **multiplies**, and multiplying always wins in the end.

steps.prompt: On which day does deal B's pay for that day first beat A's $100?
steps.hint: 2¹⁰ is about 1,000, so day 11 pays about $10. Keep doubling from there.
steps.explanation: Day n of deal B pays 0.01 × 2ⁿ⁻¹ dollars. Day 14 pays $81.92; day 15 pays **$163.84**. By day 30, B pays $5,368,709.12 in a single day, while A's whole month is $3,000.

steps.title: Race: linear vs exponential
steps.body:
This racer is borrowed from the Big-O course, so it counts *ops*: read that as *how big the number is*, and ignore the times. **O(n)** is linear (add the same), **O(n²)** grows like the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, and **O(2ⁿ)** doubles every step.

At n = 10 it's 10 vs 100 vs 1,024. Drag to n = 30: 30 vs 900 vs about **1 billion**. Switch to the **Log** scale to fit them all on screen. That gap is why *it's only doubling* is never *only*.

lessons.title: Read the numbers honestly
lessons.takeaway: Before trusting a number, check where the axis starts, ask whether it's a mean or a median, and turn counts into rates.

steps.title: Mean or median?
steps.body:
Seven bills at Juno's this morning: **$4, $5, $5, $6, $6, $7 and $90** (one catering order).

- The **mean** adds them up and divides: $123 ÷ 7 ≈ **$17.57**.
- The **median** is the middle value once sorted: **$6**.

One big order dragged the mean far above what a typical customer spends. With a few extreme values, the **median** describes the typical case better. The mean still matters when you need **totals or fair shares**, because mean × count = total.

steps.prompt: Which would you report? Sort each question.
buckets: Mean: you need a total or a fair share

items.text: The typical home price in a town with a few mansions
The typical household income in a country
The typical customer bill on a day with one $900 catering order
The typical wait for a support reply when a few tickets take weeks
How much milk to order for 30 days, from the litres used each day
Each barista's share if the week's tips are split evenly
Next week's total coffee sales, from this week's daily sales
The rent cost per cup, spreading the monthly rent over every cup sold

steps.hint: Ask: do I want *a typical case*, or do I need to *add things up or share them out*?
steps.explanation: **Typical** questions about skewed data want the **median**: a few mansions, very high incomes, a catering order or a weeks-long ticket drag the mean upward (that's why official statistics usually report median income). **Totals and fair shares** want the **mean**: 30 × the mean daily use is the milk you'll need, an even split of tips *is* the mean, and rent ÷ cups is the mean cost per cup. The median can't rebuild a total.

steps.title: Check the axis
steps.body:
Bar charts compare **lengths**, so their axis should start at **zero**. Start it higher and small differences look huge.

Juno's flyer shows her café at 102 reviews and a rival at 98, with the axis starting at 95. Her bar is 7 units tall and the rival's is 3, so hers **looks** more than twice as big. The real gap is about 4%.

Line charts may zoom in to show change, but read the axis labels before reacting to a slope.

steps.prompt: A bar chart's axis starts at **90**. Café A sold **100** cakes and Café B sold **95**. How many times taller does A's bar *look*?
steps.hint: Measure each bar from where the axis starts, not from zero.
steps.explanation: Only the part above 90 is drawn: 10 units for A and 5 for B, so A's bar looks **2×** as tall. The real ratio is 100 ÷ 95 ≈ 1.05: A sold about 5% more.

steps.title: Counts vs rates
steps.body:
Raw counts mislead when the groups differ in size. City A had **300** bike thefts last year; City B had **150**. Is A riskier?

A has 1,000,000 people and B has 200,000. Per 100,000 people, A has **30** thefts and B has **75**. Per person, B is riskier.

Whenever you see a count, ask: **out of how many?** Then compare rates: per person, per 1,000 customers, per kilometre driven.

steps.prompt: Juno's two branches: Downtown had **18** complaints from **6,000** customers; Riverside had **9** complaints from **1,500**. How many complaints per 1,000 customers at **Riverside**?
steps.explanation: 9 ÷ 1,500 × 1,000 = **6** per 1,000. Downtown: 18 ÷ 6,000 × 1,000 = 3. Riverside has half as many complaints but **twice the rate**.

steps.prompt: Rank five cafés in a chain from the **highest** complaint rate to the **lowest**.
steps.hint: Turn each into complaints per 1,000 customers before you compare.
steps.explanation: Per 1,000 customers: Hilltop **12**, Riverside **6**, Station **4**, Downtown **3**, Mall **2**. The Mall has the *most* complaints (40) but the *lowest* rate, because it serves 20,000 people. Ranking by raw counts would get it backwards.

steps.prompt: Headline: *Cycling accidents in the city hit a record high!* What's the most useful first question to ask?
choices: Did the number of people cycling, or kilometres cycled, also go up?
Which month had the most accidents?
Was last year's number also a record?
How many accidents were there in total?
steps.explanation: A count without its **denominator** can't tell you about risk. If twice as many people now cycle, a record number of accidents can still mean each trip got *safer*. The total is what the headline already gives you, and which month or whether last year was a record doesn't fix the missing denominator.

lessons.title: Ask why, five times
lessons.takeaway: Fix causes, not symptoms: keep asking why until you reach something you can change that stops the problem coming back.

steps.title: Symptom or cause?
steps.body:
Most mornings, Juno's espresso machine cuts out and she resets the circuit breaker. Problem solved… until tomorrow.

Resetting treats the **symptom**: what you notice. The **root cause** is why it keeps happening. A quick test: *if I fix this, does the problem stop coming back?*

The **5 whys**, a technique popularised at Toyota, digs down: ask *why?* about the problem, then about that answer, and so on. Five is a rule of thumb; stop when you reach a cause you can actually change.

steps.prompt: Put Juno's 5-whys chain in order, from the problem down to the root cause and its fix.
items: Problem: the espresso machine cuts out most mornings
Why? The machine and the new toaster oven draw too much power on one circuit
Why? Both are switched on at 7:00 when the café opens
Why? The opening checklist says to switch everything on at once
Fix: rewrite the checklist so machines start a few minutes apart
steps.hint: Start with what Juno notices, and make each line explain the one before it.
steps.explanation: Each line answers *why?* about the line above it. The chain ends at a **process** Juno controls: the checklist. Fixing it (or moving the toaster oven to another circuit) stops the problem for good, while resetting the breaker every morning never would.

steps.prompt: Each card is a problem and a proposed fix. Does the fix patch the symptom, or remove the root cause?

items.text: Milk runs out by noon → Theo dashes to the shop at 12
The floor by the sink is always wet → mop it more often
New staff ring up the wrong drinks → tell them to be more careful
The Wi-Fi drops every afternoon → restart the router each time
Milk runs out by noon because the standing order uses last year's numbers → base the order on this month's sales
The floor by the sink is always wet → fix the leaking pipe under the sink
New staff ring up the wrong drinks because till buttons use old names → rename the buttons to match the menu
The Wi-Fi drops when the router overheats in the sunny window → move it out of the sun

steps.hint: If you'd have to do the fix again next week, it's a patch.
steps.explanation: Apply the test: *does the problem stop coming back?* Dashing to the shop, mopping, restarting and *be more careful* all have to be repeated forever. Fixing the order numbers, the pipe, the button names or the router's spot removes the reason the problem happens. Notice that *be more careful* is a patch: people slip again, and a clearer till stops the slip for everyone.

steps.title: 5 whys, for you
steps.problem: You're late to your 9:00 class most days. Why?
steps: Why? You leave home 10 minutes late.
Why? You hit snooze several times.
Why? You're tired, because you fall asleep around 1:00.
Why? You scroll your phone in bed.
Why? It charges on the bedside table, within reach.
steps.answer: Fix the root: **charge the phone in another room**. *Try harder to be on time* only patches the symptom.

steps.prompt: A 5-whys chain at the café ends with *…because Theo forgot to restock the cups.* What's the best next step?
choices: Ask why once more: what made forgetting easy, like no checklist or no fixed restock time?
Stop: you've found who is responsible
Remind Theo to be more careful
Start a new chain about a different problem
steps.explanation: *Someone forgot* is rarely the root cause; people will slip again. Ask why once more: what made forgetting easy? A restock checklist, a fixed restock time or a low-stock alert stops the problem whoever is on shift. This is why many teams run **blameless** reviews: they look for the process gap, not the person.

steps.prompt: The cake display is often empty by 2 p.m. Juno's 5 whys led to *the baker still uses last year's order sheet.* Why might she still check other branches?
choices: Problems often have several causes, and one chain follows only one path
Because the 5 whys only works for machines
Because the first answer in a chain is usually wrong
She shouldn't: every problem has exactly one root cause
steps.explanation: The 5 whys follows **one path** down. Real problems often have several causes working together. A quick issue tree of other causes (deliveries, demand, display space) catches what a single chain misses.

units.title: Decide and deduce
units.description: Make choices you can explain, see past the first consequence, and reason through constraints.

lessons.title: Decide with a scorecard
lessons.takeaway: List real options and the criteria that matter, weight them before scoring, and move fast on reversible decisions but slow down on irreversible ones.

steps.title: Gut, meet scorecard
steps.body:
Juno needs a new espresso machine and has three quotes. Her gut likes the shiny one.

A **weighted scorecard** makes the decision explicit:

- List the real options.
- Pick the **criteria** that matter and give each a **weight** (how much it matters).
- Score each option on each criterion, say 1–5.
- Multiply each score by its weight and add up.

You don't have to obey the total blindly. But if your gut disagrees, you'll learn which criterion you *really* care about.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a weighted decision in order.
items: Write down the decision and what success looks like
List the real options (at least two)
Score every option on every criterion
Multiply, add, and compare the totals with your gut
steps.hint: You can't pick criteria until you know the goal, and you can't score until you know the criteria.
steps.explanation: Goal first, so you know what *better* means. Then options and criteria. **Weights before scores** matters most: set them before you score, so you can't quietly tune the weights to favour the option you already like. Finally, compare the total with your gut and ask why if they disagree.

steps.title: Juno's espresso machines
steps.problem:
Weights: **reliability 5, speed 3, price 2** (a higher price score means cheaper). Scores out of 5:

- **A**: reliability 4, speed 3, price 5
- **B**: reliability 5, speed 4, price 2
- **C**: reliability 3, speed 5, price 4
steps.answer: **B** wins, narrowly. The close race is information too: if B's price is a real stretch, A is nearly as good.

steps.prompt: Juno is choosing a bean supplier. Weights: **quality 0.5, price 0.3, delivery 0.2**. Supplier X scores quality 4, price 3, delivery 5. What's X's weighted score?
steps.hint: Multiply each score by its weight, then add the three results.

steps.prompt: Money gets tight, so Juno swaps two weights: **quality 0.3, price 0.5**, delivery still 0.2. Same scores: X (4, 3, 5), Y (5, 2, 3), Z (3, 5, 4). Who wins now?
choices: Z, with 4.2
X, with 3.9: the scores didn't change
Y, with 3.7
It's a tie between X and Z
steps.hint: Recompute all three with the new weights.
steps.explanation: X: 1.2 + 1.5 + 1.0 = 3.7. Y: 1.5 + 1.0 + 0.6 = 3.1. **Z: 0.9 + 2.5 + 0.8 = 4.2.** The scores didn't change, yet the winner did: the weights encode what you value, so they deserve as much thought as the scores.

steps.title: One-way and two-way doors
steps.body:
Not every decision deserves a scorecard. Amazon's Jeff Bezos sorts decisions into two kinds:

- **Two-way doors**: easy to reverse. Decide quickly, try it, learn, and walk back if it fails.
- **One-way doors**: hard or impossible to undo. Slow down, gather information, build the scorecard.

A common mistake is treating every decision as a one-way door, so even small experiments take weeks.

steps.prompt: Sort Juno's decisions.
buckets: Two-way door: decide fast, try it

items.text: Trying a new muffin flavour for a week
Changing the café playlist
Testing a 10% discount on Tuesdays
Rearranging the tables
Signing a 10-year lease on a second location
Selling the café
Taking out a large loan to buy the building
Buying a $12,000 espresso machine that can't be returned

steps.hint: Ask: if this turns out wrong, how hard is it to go back?
steps.explanation: **Two-way doors** cost little to undo: if the muffin flops or the tables feel cramped, change them back next week. Decide fast and learn from the result. **One-way doors** lock in money or commitments for years, or can't be undone at all. Those earn the slow, careful treatment, scorecard included.

lessons.title: And then what? Second-order effects
lessons.takeaway: Every decision has consequences of consequences: ask *and then what?* at least twice before you act, especially when you reward a number.

steps.title: And then what?
steps.body:
Juno offers **free refills**. The first-order effect: happy customers. Now ask *and then what?* People stay longer, tables stay full at lunch, and new customers see no seats and walk out.

**First-order effects** are the direct, intended results. **Second-order effects** are the consequences of those consequences. They're easy to miss because they arrive later, hit other people, or show up in another part of the business.

steps.prompt: Juno halves the latte price for a month. Put the chain of effects in order.
items: The 8 a.m. queue gets much longer
Some regulars give up waiting and buy coffee elsewhere
Morning revenue can fall even though more lattes are sold
steps.hint: Start with the decision itself; each later card should be caused by the one before.
steps.explanation: Each effect causes the next. The first-order effect (more lattes sold) looks like success; the second- and third-order effects (longer queues, lost regulars) can cancel it out. Asking *and then what?* twice would have flagged the queue before launch.

steps.prompt: Juno launches a loyalty card: every 10th coffee free. Sort each effect.

items.text: Card holders get every 10th coffee free
Juno pays to print the cards
Card holders pay a little less per coffee on average
Regulars pick Juno's over the café next door, to fill their card
The café next door launches its own loyalty card
Stamping cards slows the till, so the queue moves more slowly

steps.hint: Is it the rule itself, or someone's reaction to the rule?
steps.explanation: **First-order** effects follow directly from the rule itself: free coffees, printing costs, a lower average price. **Second-order** effects come from how people *react*: customers change where they go, the rival responds, and a new task slows the till. The reactions are where the surprises live.

steps.title: Incentives bite back
steps.body:
Second-order effects hit hardest when you **reward a number**. In 1902, officials in colonial Hanoi paid a bounty for every rat tail handed in. Soon tail-less rats were seen in the streets: people cut off the tails and let the rats go on breeding.

The lesson is often summed up as **Goodhart's law**: when a measure becomes a target, people chase the measure instead of the goal behind it.

steps.prompt: Juno plans a bonus for baristas based on **drinks served per hour**. What's the most likely second-order effect?
choices: Rushed drinks and fewer chats with customers, as staff chase speed
Nothing changes except that staff work faster at the same quality
Baristas start pushing customers toward pricier drinks
Customers start ordering more drinks each visit
steps.explanation: People optimise what's measured. A speed bonus rewards speed, so care, latte art and chats with regulars, none of which is counted, tend to slip. Pushing pricier drinks is what a *sales* bonus would encourage, not a speed bonus. Pairing speed with a quality check, like complaints or remade drinks, limits the gaming.

steps.prompt: Juno raises the latte price from **$4 to $5**. She sells **400** lattes a week. First-order thinking says revenue goes from $1,600 to $2,000. But **30%** of those customers switch to filter coffee at **$3**. What's the new weekly revenue from these 400 customers?
steps.hint: Split the 400 into those who keep buying lattes and those who switch.
steps.explanation: 70% keep buying lattes: 280 × $5 = $1,400. 30% switch: 120 × $3 = $360. Total **$1,760**. Still up $160 on $1,600, but well short of the $400 gain the first-order guess promised.

lessons.title: Deduce it: the rota puzzle
lessons.takeaway: With constraints, list what's possible, let each clue cross options out, and when you're stuck, try one case and see if it breaks.

steps.title: Cross things out
steps.body:
Juno is planning next week's staff rota. Puzzles like this give way to **elimination**: list every possibility, then let each clue cross some out. Two moves do most of the work:

- **Only one left**: if someone fits just one slot, they get it, and nobody else can have it.
- **If-then clues**: *if P then Q* only rules out the case where P is true and Q is false.

That second one trips people up, so check it with a truth table.

steps.prompt: Clue: *If Theo opens (P), then Mia closes (Q).* Fill in when the clue holds (T) and when it's broken (F). Then do the same for its **contrapositive**: *if Mia doesn't close, Theo doesn't open.*

columns.label: If not Q then not P

steps.hint: An if-then promise is only broken when the *if* part happens and the *then* part doesn't.
steps.explanation: The clue is broken in just one row: **Theo opens but Mia doesn't close** (P true, Q false). When Theo doesn't open, the clue makes no promise, so it holds. The contrapositive column comes out identical: it's the same rule read backwards. So once you know Mia isn't closing, you can cross out Theo opening.

steps.prompt: Rota clue: *Theo works the day after Mia* (the days are Monday to Thursday). Which can you cross out straight away?
choices: Theo on Monday
Theo on Thursday
Mia on Monday
Mia on Wednesday
steps.explanation: Theo needs Mia on the day before his, and nobody works the day before Monday, so **Theo can't be on Monday**. By the same logic Mia can't be on Thursday. The other options are still possible until more clues arrive.

steps.title: A warm-up rota
steps.problem: Theo, Mia and Sam each take one shift: morning, afternoon or evening. Clues: (1) Mia doesn't work mornings. (2) Sam works a later shift than Mia.
steps: Clue 1 crosses out Mia–morning, so Mia is afternoon or evening.
Clue 2 says someone works later than Mia, so Mia can't be evening. **Mia = afternoon.**
Sam must be later than afternoon: **Sam = evening.**
Only one left: **Theo = morning.**
steps.answer: Each clue removed options until every slot had exactly one name left.

steps.prompt: You've applied every clue directly, but several cells are still open. What's the best next move?
choices: Assume one possibility, follow the clues, and cross it out if it leads to a contradiction
Guess the most likely answer and move on
Conclude the puzzle must have more than one solution
Re-read only the first clue until something new appears
steps.explanation: **Try a case.** Pick a clue with only two possibilities, assume one, and follow the clues. If it leads to a contradiction, cross it out: the other case must be true. Guessing skips the reasoning, and a well-made puzzle with open cells usually just needs this extra step, not a verdict that it has several answers.

steps.prompt: Juno's rota: four people, four days, four jobs. Each person works one day and does one job. Who works when, doing what?
clues: Theo works exactly two days after Sam.
Whoever bakes works on Monday, so the bread is fresh for the week.
Juno does neither the deliveries nor the cleaning.
Mia works earlier in the week than Juno.
The deliveries happen later in the week than the till shift.
steps.hint: Clue 1 leaves only two possible day pairs for Sam and Theo. Combine it with clue 4 and test each case against clue 5.
steps.explanation: Clue 1 leaves two cases: Sam Monday and Theo Wednesday, or Sam Tuesday and Theo Thursday. Clue 4 then fills the other two days: in case 1 Mia gets Tuesday and Juno Thursday; in case 2 Mia gets Monday and Juno Wednesday. Clue 2 puts the baker on Monday, which is never Juno, so by clue 3 **Juno is on the till**. In case 1 Juno's till shift is Thursday, and clue 5 needs deliveries later than that: impossible. So it's case 2: **Mia** bakes on Monday, **Juno** is on the till on Wednesday, **Theo** does deliveries on Thursday (the only day after Wednesday), and **Sam** cleans on Tuesday.
